When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside.

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won’t forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let’s get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.

#1422. Winning is the only thing that matters to Rangers midfielder Dan Neil as Ibrox club continue to gain momentum in title challenge

Published: 13:52 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 14:02 EST, 8 November 2026

Rangers midfielder Dan Neil admits he couldn’t care less about how his side go about picking up points as long as the wins keep coming.

The stand-in captain netted the crucial second in Saturday’s hard-fought victory over St Mirren in Paisley after Ryan Naderi had given the visitors a first-half lead from the penalty spot.

It was a result which extended Rangers’ unbeaten run to 12 in all competitions as they continue to build momentum following an unconvincing start to the campaign, and Neil insists that’s the only thing that matters at this stage.

He said: ‘I think every good team just finds a way to win.

‘Obviously, we’d like to win by four or five goals every single week but unfortunately that’s just not football. I do think it’s an area that we can improve on.

‘There’s been too many games this year where maybe we don’t get that second goal and it’s a bit nervy. Teams get a little bit of confidence off that and the momentum shifts.

Dan Neil savours the moment after putting the seal on Rangers' win with the second goal

‘I think it’s definitely something that we can improve on, putting teams to bed when we do go 1-0 up and go 1-0 up early doors when we’re creating chances.

‘But at the same time, finding a way to win is the most important way and whether that’s 1-0 or 5-0, at the end of the day it’s three points.’

While Rangers weren’t quite at their best in Paisley, they did more than enough to halt their poor recent run away from home.

Back-to-back 2-2 draws at Dundee and Hearts last month saw valuable points dropped in what is shaping up to be a tight title race, and Neil was delighted to get back to winning ways ahead of the international break.

‘The last two away results and performances really haven’t been us,’ said the former Sunderland man. ‘It was important that we didn’t have another one of them going into the break and have it lingering over us. Everyone played their part in making it a comfortable result.

‘Coming away from home in any league is tough, but especially this league. It’s important that the mentality of the group is right, which it is, and I think you’ve seen that on Saturday night.

‘It was important to put that hoodoo of those two results behind us and make sure that we win the game. I think there was some good football played for the majority of the game and we also dug in when we had to. That’s credit to every single player in that dressing room.’

#1421. South Korean star Kim Min-su has no goals and no assists, but it's no problem for Rangers boss Derek McInnes

Published: 14:24 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 14:24 EST, 8 November 2026

Kim Min-su’s stat sheet since making the big-money move to Rangers over the summer should be the kind of thing that makes a manager legitimately wonder if both he and the club have been taken for a ride.

Twelve games, zero goals, zero assists. A rank-rotten return, on the face of it. So why does Derek McInnes not seem even remotely concerned by the whole palaver?

Well, simply put, he has a set of eyes. He, like everyone else, can clearly see that the South Korean is the heartbeat of everything that has been good about Rangers in an attacking sense ever since he was thrown into the team – even if the numbers don’t quite back it up.

It was the same story in yesterday’s hard-fought – but deserved – 2-0 win away at St Mirren.

It was hard to keep track of the number of times Min-su drifted in from the left-hand side to pick up possession with no opposition player within five yards. That’s not luck, it’s intelligence.

There is nobody playing in Scotland’s top flight more adept at taking the ball on the turn and driving into space either.

South Korean Kim Min-su contributes to all that is good about Rangers' attacking work

Min-su made life difficult for St Mirren during Rangers' 2-0 victory over the Paisley side

Dan Neil scores Rangers' second in a win that keeps them within four points of leaders Celtic

St Mirren couldn’t get near him for the majority of the first hour. They aren’t the first side to experience such difficulties, and they won’t be the last.

In full flight, he is a joy to watch operating in that pocket between the opposition midfield and defence.

It’s the bit after that where things start to become a little trickier for the talented 20-year-old.

He squandered a couple of opportunities to open his account here. The first came after playing a neat one-two with James Penrice late in the first half, with the ball sitting up perfectly for him ten yards out to smash home.

The choice to take one touch too many allowed Declan John to clear the danger.

So much of his game is based on instinct. Indeed, it’s a big part of what makes him such captivating viewing. But his decision-making in front of goal needs a lot of work.

Perhaps he’s guilty of overthinking things too much.

His manager certainly thinks so, admitting post-match that he felt Min-su was becoming ‘obsessed’ with registering his first goal for the club. In key moments, that shows.

A heavy touch early in the second period after being played in by Badredine Bouanani – unusually quiet here on the right – once again suggested he is feeling the pressure.

But let’s not forget, he’s essentially a kid trying to find his feet in a new country, and in a league which couldn’t be more different in terms of speed and style from what he was used to in Spain.

That he has actually managed to settle in so seamlessly should be applauded. It can’t have been an easy transition but he has quickly endeared himself to the supporters.

It’s why they are every bit as desperate as the player himself to get the monkey off his back.

They needn’t worry. If he keeps doing what he’s doing, the goals will come. Of that there is no doubt.

Some context has to be attached to his failure to notch an assist too. It’s a misleading stat, given that it depends entirely on someone else putting the ball away when it counts.

Min-su created multiple chances for his team-mates in Paisley, the best of which saw Kevin Kelsy put through on goal. It’s hardly his fault that the big man fluffed his lines. The Venezuelan has been in good form but had a stinker here.

At some point, everything will come together for Min-su. And it’s not as if he didn’t have an impact in both of Rangers’ goals against St Mirren.

It may have gone unnoticed amongst everything else, but he absolutely busted a gut to get himself into the box in the build-up to Dan Neil’s deflected strike which sealed the points on 61 minutes. That willingness to put the hard yards in off the ball is every bit as impressive as his ability on it.

And it was his pass to Penrice which led to the full-back being clipped by Samuel Ramos inside the box to give Rangers the opportunity to go ahead from the penalty spot early in the first half.

In truth, they may have been a little fortunate to do so. Put it this way, had referee Nick Walsh not given it, there’s not a chance in hell that VAR would have got involved.

Ryan Naderi stepped up to slot into the bottom corner to take his tally to nine for the season in all competitions.

It says a lot about where Naderi's head is that he had the confidence to do so, especially after blowing a great chance from six yards out only moments before. The German-born Czech international is a changed man, all right.

Speaking of confidence, there is no shortage of it at the other end of the park either. At times, the defensive pairing of Olwethu Makhanya and Emmanuel Fernandez look like they’re playing five-a-sides.

It’s usually the latter who throws in the odd lapse of concentration to add some peril to proceedings, but yesterday it was the normally dependable Makhanya’s turn to give his manager a few hairy moments. Thankfully for the South African, St Mirren couldn’t take advantage.

Craig McLeish’s men could have no complaints over the final result but could have made things interesting late on had either Eseosa Sule or Calvin Ramsay finished from close range.

It’s now just one win in nine for the Buddies, who – much like last season – just can’t seem to put the ball in the back of the net consistently. That problem plagued them so much that they ended up in the relegation play-off spot last year.

McLeish has done an excellent job since taking over from Stephen Robinson. A far better one than anyone could have possibly predicted. He has changed the style of this team completely in a very short space of time and so you have to trust he will be able to find a solution to their goalscoring issues too.

Rangers might be 13 points better off but they head into the international break also in search of that perfect balance.

When they’re on it, they’re very good. But they are still not commanding games from start to finish with any sort of regularity.

They won’t necessarily have to be pleasing on the eye to end up with their hands on the Premiership trophy come May. Celtic’s triumph last season proved that.

The Rangers supporters will gladly put up with imperfect displays for the next six months if that’s going to be the end result.

And if the likes of Min-su can hit the goal trail sometime soon, there’s a decent chance that’s exactly how things will play out.

#1420. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

Fabian Hurzeler’s side have made an excellent start to the Premier League season, sitting third with 18 goals scored in six matches, and will hope to replicate their domestic form in this European encounter against Lithuanian minnows Kauno Zalgiris.

English clubs have won the Conference League in three of the five seasons since the competition’s creation, with Brighton’s bitter rivals Crystal Palace previously lifting the trophy in May.

Hurzeler has made eight changes to the team which beat Sunderland last Saturday, with Jack Hinshelwood notably returning to the line-up.

Whatever the result, this is a momentous night for Bournemouth, who are poised for their first European fixture at home in the club’s history as they welcome Austrian outfit Sturm Graz to the Vitality Stadium.

Bournemouth kickstarted their inaugural Europa League campaign with an unforgettable 2-1 victory over Real Sociedad on September 17 in San Sebastian, thanks to first-half goals from Justin Kluivert and Rayan.

This was just Bournemouth’s second win of the season in all competitions, with the club having made a slow start to the campaign under new head coach Marco Rose. That other triumph arrived in the EFL Cup, when Bournemouth thrashed Lincoln City 4-0 at the start of September.

The buzz around Bournemouth’s European exploits have partially masked a very poor opening to the Premier League season as Rose’s winless side languish in 18th, with only three points from six games. They suffered a heavy 5-1 loss to Chelsea at Stamford Bridge in their previous outing.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

#1419. Celtic 1 Kilmarnock 0: Liam Scales scores only goal as Premiership leaders make hard work of it

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 15:06 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 15:06 EST, 8 November 2026

For Martin O’Neill, the second international break of the season should be somewhat less fretful than the first.

Seven weeks ago, with a home defeat to Ferencvaros coming in between two no-shows against Rangers, the veteran wondered aloud if it might be time to ‘wrap it up’.

O’Neill later admitted that he regretted his choice of words. He won’t, though, lament the decision to go again as he rests up in the coming days.

While the intervening weeks have often been a bumpy ride, the past four days have been a lot more like it.

Thursday’s dramatic win over Besiktas has breathed new life into Celtic’s Europa League campaign.

While by no means spectacular, this narrow victory over Kilmarnock re-established their four-point lead at the top of the Premiership and will have further dampened the sense of hysteria which was threatening to engulf the entire club.

Celtic defender Liam Scales loops the ball over Kilmarnock's goalkeeper and into the net

Scales celebrates with Camilo Duran after netting the only goal of the game at Celtic Park

Celtic striker Kasper Hogh finds the net with a crisp right-foot shot, only to have it disallowed

Celtic certainly made hard work of this. Truth be told, they should have gone into the break on the back of a far more convincing victory.

While they were right to feel wronged that Kasper Hogh saw his goalless run stretch to 16 matches after having one harshly disallowed, O’Neill’s men did not help themselves either.

Coming after Liam Scales had given them a half-time advantage, Benjamin Nygren’s missed penalty allowed Kilmarnock to keep believing right to the end.

Nonetheless, it was hard to begrudge Celtic their victory over the piece. A few weeks back, this might have been a contest in which they’d have come a cropper. They look more assured defensively than earlier in the season.

You don’t need to stay up all night researching exactly why Kilmarnock are in such peril at this stage of the season.

Neil McCann’s side began the campaign losing goals and they’ve really never stopped. They cough up more chances than any side in the top division. When it comes to shooting themselves in the foot, they’re in a league of their own.

In 13 games to date, they’ve shipped 29 goals and have kept just two clean sheets in the process. St Mirren, the side with the second worst record in the Premiership, have lost 22.

As worrying as those statistics and the Premiership table undoubtedly are, though, this felt like a step in the right direction.

In being more resolute, McCann’s men stayed in the contest right until the final whistle. They fashioned a number of decent chances throughout. There was plenty of encouragement here, even though they went down again.

For the home supporters, the much-needed positivity which had emanated from Thursday’s European win was boosted by the return to the starting line-up of Jota for the first time since April 2025.

Notably, only three out of nine of Celtic’s summer signings made the squad, with Sam Johnstone the only one involved who arrived on deadline day.

O’Neill was indebted to the on-loan Wolves man inside the first minute. Ieuan Owen skipped away from Callum McGregor then Colby Donovan down the left and put in a dangerous cross. Twice Tom Lowery hit the target. Twice the Celtic keeper stood up tall.

Lowery immediately had his name taken by John Beaton for a clumsy foul on Nygren.

Despite their precarious position, to their credit, Kilmarnock didn’t come to Parkhead just to defend. Tyreece John-Jules, their main striker, had an abundance of support in the form of Owen, Greg Kiltie and Joe Hugill.

Between them, they fashioned enough half chances. They just didn’t have ice in the veins at the right moments.

Hogh was right to feel aggrieved at the decision which cost him that elusive goal. Truthfully, there was very little in Mika Baur’s challenge on Kiltie which was retrospectively penalised.

Duran gathered and fed Nygren. The Swede swivelled and rolled the ball into Hogh’s path. A crisp right-foot finish was not that of a player lacking in confidence.

The Dane’s lengthy celebrations included a look up to the heavens. By the time Beaton made his way to the monitor and chalked the goal off, Hogh could have been forgiven for feeling that someone up there had it in for him.

To Hogh’s credit, he didn’t let it affect him. Moments later, after being played in by Duran, he was only denied his revenge by the outstretched leg of Nico Mantl.

Hogh then played Duran in with a clever back-heel. The Colombian lashed his effort just wide.

Celtic’s pressure was mounting and they edged in front on 26 minutes with Duran, yet again excellent throughout, the architect.

His clipped cross from the right caught the Kilmarnock defence flat-footed. Scales extended his left foot and watched the ball rise to the point where it appeared to be going over.

With Mantl hoping that it would clear his bar, it looped into the net. There was no disputing this one.

Required to take more risks, Killie had to be careful when they turned the ball over. Hugill and Cathal McCarthy were both booked for crude fouls on Duran and Jota, respectively.

While Celtic began to control the affair, the visitors were not without their moments. Michael Schjonning-Larsen’s stinging strike from 25 yards forced Johnstone into another solid stop.

While Jota looked good in moments, it’s clearly going to take some time before he’s fully up to speed. The same might apply to Hyun-jun Yang, the man who replaced him at the interval, after being sidelined for six weeks with a hamstring injury.

Donovan came close to wrapping up the three points with an enterprising run and shot with his left foot which flew just wide.

Duran’s close control and speed across the ground bought him a yard for a shot. Having seen it late, Mantl dealt with it well.

Hogh actually performed well here. He was tidy with the ball and frequently brought team-mates into play. He just didn’t hit the target often enough. That again cost him when he spun neatly in the box and tried his luck midway through the second period.

You couldn’t fault him when he seized on Kieran Tierney’s cross, though. The saving block from Killie substitute MJ Kamson-Kamara was tremendous.

With the home supporters longing for a clinching second goal, Duran dumped a shot into the side netting before the industrious Baur was flagged offside after firing home.

The wait would go on. Initially adjudged to have struck Aaron Tshibola’s arm just outside the box, Yang’s strike would earn Celtic a spot-kick with 14 minutes remaining after a VAR review.

Nygren just never looked confident as he spotted the ball. Mantl dived to his right and made a comfortable save. Those hoping for a sharp exit sat back in their seats.

The sight of Baur hobbling badly after being caught by Tshibola didn’t make the viewing in the final moments any easier. All that truly counted for the home fans, though, was that Celtic got over the line.

#1418. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1417. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

Kick-offs in our three 3pm fixtures are moments away as players emerge from tunnels at grounds across the country.

The Etihad has gone bananas. The inflatables are all over the ground and it is believed that demand has exceeded supply. The image on the front of the matchday programme is of the inflatable bananas on the terraces, just like 40 years ago when the craze first started.

Aug 24: Fulham 2 Chelsea 3 Aug 30: Sunderland 1 Fulham 0Sep 5: Fulham 2 Crystal Palace 3Sep 12: Liverpool 0 Fulham 0Sep 20: Fulham 1 Manchester United 1Oct 10: Ipswich Town 2 Fulham 1

One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

However, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

It’s back-to-back wins for Chelsea and a rare clean sheet, their first since January. But all thoughts will be with Emi Martinez after his clash of heads with Branthwaite. Hopefully we get some good news on that front soon. Follow the latest updates here.

Enzo Maresca has been looking for opportunities for rest his key players - but Erling Haaland is a player that is impossible to rest. He has scored in his last seven matches and leads Manchester City’s attack again.

But Maresca has changed half of his team from the line-up defeated by Paris St-Germain in the week. Jeremy Doku and City’s first-choice centre-backs are the others to keep their place. The rest are drafted in to face Ipswich, with Matheus Nunes, Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Iliman Ndiaye and Mateo Kovačić are drafted in.

There is also a place for Phil Foden after serving his three-match ban for getting dismissed in the Manchester derby.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Manchester City’s claim to have “irrefutable evidence” that will overturn their guilty verdict on appeal is based on a trove of emails, letters and bank statements.

A re-examination of Abu Dhabi government documents, receipts and testimony from 24 witnesses – all of which the club believe were wrongly dismissed at the original hearing – will be central in attempts to force a full or partial acquittal or retrial, according to people familiar with the case.

City’s legal team will attempt to demonstrate “fundamental errors” in tests applied by an independent commission to the Premier League’s case that commercial revenue was artificially inflated by £920m. Sources with understanding of City’s case have told Telegraph Sport the club are bullish about their appeal, based on:

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1416. In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells1,2,3,4. Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells5,6,7,8,9. These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1–SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer.

All data generated or analysed in this study are included in this article, its Supplementary Information, source data files and Supplementary Datasets, or are available through public repositories. Raw and processed high-throughput sequencing data generated in this study, including CRISPR screen sequencing, targeted amplicon sequencing, bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, CUT&RUN and WGS data, have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus under the accession numbers GSE272887 and GSE335215, and the Sequence Read Archive under the accession number PRJNA1477126. Source data and statistical information for non-high-throughput experiments, including flow cytometry, protein analyses, imaging analyses and other molecular or cellular assays, are provided with this paper as source data files. Processed results and relevant quantifications from high-throughput experiments are provided in the Supplementary Datasets. The following publicly available reference datasets and resources were used in this study: the human reference genome GRCh38 Gencode v44 for bulk RNA-seq analyses; the human reference genome GRCh38 Gencode v37 for single-cell RNA-seq analyses; the human reference genome GRCh38 Gencode v47 and ENCODE blacklist regions for GRCh38 for WGS analyses; the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB v7.4); and the ProjecTILs single-cell T cell atlas dataset. Parental cell lines are available from the commercial sources listed in the Methods and Supplementary Information. Engineered cell lines, plasmids and other research materials generated in this study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request and completion of any required material transfer agreements. Source data are provided with this paper.

Custom code used for data analysis and figure generation in this study is available at GitHub (https://github.com/Prenauer/DKO-CAR-T).

a, Quantification of CD3− cells 5 days after CRISPR-mediated gene editing in three independent donors. b, Quantification of live cells 5 days after editing with the indicated Cas9 mRNA concentrations, n = 3 biologically independent replicates. Data are shown as mean + s.e.m. Significance was calculated using one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test. ns, not significant. c, Left, representative flow cytometry plots showing CD3 and CD28 protein-level DKO efficiency in activated human primary T cells 5 days after Cas9 mRNA electroporation. Right, quantification of CD3+ CD28+ cells in DKO and vector control groups; data are shown as mean + s.e.m.; n = 4 infection replicates. Significance was calculated using a paired two-sided t-test, ****P < 0.0001. d, Quantification of CD3− or CD28− cells 5 days after editing; n = 3 donors per concentration. Data are shown as mean ± s.e.m. e, Classification and composition of targeted genes in the T cell DKO CRISPR library. f, Schematic of the two-step T cell DKO CRISPR library construction process. g, Quantification of plasmid library sgRNA-pair construct distribution. h, Flow cytometry histograms showing EGFRvIII expression in U87-GL and U87-GL-EGFRvIII cell lines. i, Flow cytometry histograms showing PD-L1 expression in U87-GL and U87-GL-EGFRvIII cell lines. j, Schematic of DKO CAR-T cell library generation pipeline, including human T cell isolation and activation, CAR-T cell generation and selection, lentiviral DKO CRISPR library infection and Cas9 mRNA electroporation. Schematic in panel j created in BioRender; Chen, S. https://biorender.com/4g9xapi (2026). k, Spider plots of tumour volumes for donor 1 in vivo screen experiment shown in Fig. 1d. n = 5 biologically independent mice. l, Representative H&E-stained tumour sections from two biologically independent tumours per group from the screen shown in Fig. 1c. Scale bar, 250 μm. m, sgRNA-pair detection rates from the total library across individual samples. D, donor; T, tumour. n, Heat map of Spearman correlation coefficients between the log2-normalized counts-per-million (log-norm.) sgRNA counts for each sample. Data were arranged by hierarchical clustering using the ward.D2 method. o, Multidimensional scaling analysis of log2-normalized screen data using the top 10,000 most variable sgRNA pairs across samples. Data points were clustered by k-means. p, Box-dot plot of library representation across individual samples, showing the distribution of all sgRNA-pair constructs counts. Boxes indicate the 25th–75th percentiles, center lines indicate medians, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Individual points represent sgRNA-pair counts. q, Empirical cumulative distribution function of DKO library representation among detected sgRNA pairs in plasmid, pre-injection cell and tumour samples. Sample labels in m-p indicate sample type, plasmid, pre-injection cell or tumour, and donor ID.

a, Distribution of the top four performing sgRNA-pair constructs for top DKO hits across samples, ranked by SAMBA sgRNA z-score. b, Heat map of DKO screen scores for all pairwise gene combinations assessed in the CRISPR screen. Values were scaled and visualized within a range of −1 to 1. Hierarchical clustering was performed using the Ward.D2 method based on Euclidean distances. c, Scatter plot showing the relationship between screen enrichment and synergistic effect. SAMBA z-scores were plotted against synergy scores for each gene pair. Dashed lines indicate FDR-adjusted P value, q < 0.05, for epistasis and SAMBA results. d, Scatter plot of observed DKO SAMBA scores versus expected SAMBA scores based on the additive effects of the corresponding SKOs for each gene pair (SKO1 + SKO2). Points are colored by synergy score. Linear regression yielded R2 = 0.0152 (n = 2,485 gene pairs; 71 SKO genes), indicating minimal predictability of DKO outcomes from SKO additivity. e, Quantification of indel frequencies in DKO-edited CAR-T cells 5 days after electroporation across three independent batches. P values were calculated using unpaired two-sided t-tests. Data are mean ± s.e.m.; n = 3 human donors. Each dot represents one human donor. f, Quantification of indel frequencies in CAR-T cells from three donors generated across three independent batches 90 days after gene editing. P values were calculated using one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test versus GTC. Data are mean + s.e.m.; n = 3 independent donor-derived CAR-T cell preparations, generated from three donors in independent batches. NS, not significant, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001.

a, Quantification of live cells 5 days after editing in different DKO CAR-T cells compared with controls, n = 3 infection replicates per group. b, Schematic of generation of DKO CAR-T or CAR-Jurkat cell generation and downstream assays. Schematic in panel b created in BioRender; Chen, S. https://biorender.com/7vyyd1r (2026). c, Quantification of Ca2+ flux AUC and peak signal change in different DKO CAR-Jurkat samples. The resting region was defined as 1 min before antigen crosslinking, and the peak region was defined as 500 s after cross-linking. AUC is calculated as (mean peak signal – mean resting signal) × 500. Representative of three independent experiments. d, Quantification of pERK1/2 (pT202/pY204) signal in DKO CAR-Jurkat cells after U87-GL-EGFRvIII stimulation at the indicated time points; n = 3 per group per time point. e, Quantification of pERK1/2+ (pT202/pY204) DKO CAR-T cells after U87-GL-EGFRvIII cell stimulation for 30 min; n = 3 biological replicates per group. f-g, NF-κB CFP and NFAT/AP-1 GFP reporter activity after coculture of U87-GL-EGFRvIII cells with different DKO CD8+ CAR-Jurkat cells with GTC control at indicated time points. E:T = 1:2. n = 3 per group per time point. f, Schematic of the NFAT/AP-1 GFP reporter structure and quantification of GFP+ cells. g, Schematic of the NF-κB CFP reporter structure and the quantification of CFP+ cells. h, Quantifications of tonic signaling in CAR-Jurkat cells after 1 month cell culture without stimulation, n = 3. P value was determined by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s correction for multiple comparisons test versus GTC. i, Left, representative flow cytometry histograms showing CD107a expression in CD8+ DKO and GTC CAR-T cells after 2-h coculture with U87-GL-EGFRvIII cells. Right, quantification of CD107a+ CAR-T cells; n = 4 per group; E:T = 1:2. j, Quantification of IFN-γ, TNF, and granzyme B expression in CD8+ and CD4+ CAR-T cells after 4-h coculture with U87-GL-EGFRvIII cells at E:T = 1:8; n = 4 per group. k, Left, quantification of CellTrace Violetlow CAR-T cells after two rounds of repeated antigen stimulation, measured on day 5, n = 6 each. Right, quantification of absolute CAR-T cell numbers; n = 3 on day 0, n = 6 on day 2, 5, and 7 per group. l, Quantification of CellTrace Violetlow CAR-T cells in low IL-2 medium, measured on day 7; n = 3 per group. m, Quantification of live cells percentage in culture or after repeated challenge. n, Left, quantification of CD45RO+ CD62L+ DKO CAR-T cells after two rounds of tumour stimulation on day 5. Right, quantification of CD27+ DKO CAR-T cells after two rounds of tumour stimulation on day 5; n = 6 per group. For each round of coculture, E:T = 1:4. o, Quantifications of LAG-3, PD-1, and TIM-3 expression in CAR-T cells after repeated tumour challenge on day 5, n = 4 per group. For each round of coculture, E:T = 1:4. p, Quantification of LAG-3+, PD-1+, TIM-3+ CAR-T cells after two rounds of tumour stimulation on day 5; n = 4 per group. For each round of coculture, E:T = 1:4. q, SPICE analysis of LAG-3, PD-1, and TIM-3 expression in CAR-T cells on day 5. Data are group means. r, Quantification of absolute CAR-T cell number after IL-2 withdrawal; n = 3 per group at day 0, n = 4 per group at day 2, 5, and 7. Data in d-g,k right,m,r are mean ± s.e.m.; data in a,h-j,k left,l,n-p are mean + s.e.m. Significance levels were calculated using ordinary two-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test comparing each group with GTC within each row or time point (d-g,j,k right,m,r), repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test versus GTC (a), or ordinary one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test versus GTC (h,i,k left,l,n-p). Dashed lines in c, i, j, n-p indicate mean values of the GTC group. n indicates biologically independent samples unless otherwise stated. Exact P values and detailed statistics are provided in the Source Data. Data are representative of three independent experiments using cells from human donors independent of those used in the screen. NS, not significant, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001.

a, Schematic of the time-series RNA-seq experiment in DKO, NR4A1 SKO, SOCS3 SKO, and GTC CAR-T cells undergoing repeated tumour challenges. b, Principal components analysis (PCA) of all RNA-seq samples across all stimulation time-points (left) or separated by timepoint (right). The first two principal components are shown. Genotypes are indicated by dot color, and samples are grouped by time point (left) or genotype (right) using convex hulls. c, Volcano plots of differential expression (DE) analysis for epistasis at each time-point. Significant epistatic transcripts were defined by an FDR-adjusted P value (q value) <0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change (LFC) > 0.5 for the DKO interaction term in the statistical model (Methods). Top DE transcripts are labeled based on significance and LFC, with selected transcripts shown in bold. d, Heatmaps and pathway analysis of DE transcripts from pairwise comparisons between genotypes across stimulation times. For each time point, DE transcripts were hierarchically clustered and shown as heatmaps (left). Pathway analyses were performed independently for each transcript cluster using over-representation analysis (ORA) tests with MSIGDB v7.4 Hallmark gene-sets. Significant pathways (q < 0.05; up to four pathways per cluster shown) are shown on the right, color-coded by the transcript clusters. Dot-size indicates the percentage of pathway genes that were significantly differentially expressed. e, Heatmaps of DE transcripts significantly enriched as NF-κB and STAT5B targets by transcription factor (TF) over-representation analysis (ORA). TF analysis was performed using MSIGDB v7.4 TF gene-sets; ontology names are shown above the heatmaps. f-g, Representative flow cytometry histogram and quantification of p-STAT3 and p-STAT5 in CAR-T cell groups. n = 4 (f), and n = 3 (g) biological replicates per group. h, Representative flow cytometry histograms and quantification of BAX expression in CAR-T cells. n = 3 biological replicates per group. Data in f-h are mean + s.e.m. Significance levels in f-h were calculated using one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons versus GTC (f-g) or DKO (h). Exact P values and detailed statistics are provided in the Source Data. NS, not significant, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001.

a, Schematic of the single-cell transcriptomics (SCT) data processing pipeline. b, UMAP projections showing the T cell filtering step in the SCT analysis. B cells were identified by CD20 expression, and T cells were identified by CD3E expression. c, Dot plot showing gene signatures used for immune subset classification. Cells were classified into major immune cell categories, CD8+ T cell subsets and phenotypic states. Dot color and size indicate average gene signature z-score and percentage of expressing cells. Gene-sets used for each gene signature of the dot plot are shown in the right panel tables. d, Dot plot showing transcriptional patterns of marker genes used to classify in vivo CAR-T cell subsets in the SCT data. Dot color and size indicate average gene expression z-score and percentage of expressing cells. e, Distribution of ungrouped T cell subsets across genotypes, shown as stacked bar plots (left) and quantified by subset (right). Cells from mice within each treatment group were pooled before single-cell RNA sequencing. Statistical comparisons of cell-subset proportions between genotypes were performed using two-sided pairwise Fisher’s exact tests with Holm adjustment for multiple comparisons. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001. f, Dot plot showing transcriptional patterns for genes comprising signatures of key T cell signaling pathways and functions. Dot color and size indicate average gene expression z-score and percentage of expressing cells, respectively. Data are arranged by hierarchical clustering using the ward.D2 method, and dashed boxes mark DKO subsets.

a, PCA projections of in vivo CAR-T cells grouped by genotype and subset, based on gene expression patterns for each gene-set. PCA was performed using the gene expression data shown in Extended Data Fig. 7f. Points are color-coded by genotype, and polygons mark DKO subset points that clustered together. b, Volcano plots of differential transcription factor signature analysis between DKO and GTC genotypes. Upregulated and downregulated signatures, defined by adjusted P < 0.01 and absolute log2 fold change > 0.25, are shown as red and blue dots, respectively. Statistical comparisons were performed using cell-level Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, and P values were adjusted for multiple testing using Bonferroni correction. c, Dot plot showing transcriptional patterns for genes comprising transcription factor signatures. Dot color and size indicate average gene expression z-score and percentage of expressing cells. Data are arranged by hierarchical clustering using the ward.D2 method, and dashed boxes mark DKO subsets. d, PCA projection of in vivo CAR-T cells grouped by genotype and subset, based on gene expression patterns for each gene-set. PCA was performed using the gene expression data shown in c. Points are color-coded by genotype, and polygons mark DKO subset points that clustered together. e, Left, representative flow cytometry MitoTracker Green signal. Right, quantification of MitoTracker Green MFI; n = 4 per group. CAR-T cells were stimulated with U87-GL-EGFRvIII cells at E:T = 1:1 and cultured for 7 days. f, Left, OCR curves from Seahorse assays. Right, quantification of SRC and MRC; n = 3 per group. g, Illustration of epistasis involving PGC-1α downstream of NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO. Data in f left are mean ± s.e.m., in e,f right are mean +s.e.m. Significance levels were calculated using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (e) or two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (f). n indicates biologically independent samples. CAR-T cells were generated using human donor cells independent of those used in the screen. Exact P values and detailed statistics are provided in the Source Data. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001. OCR, oxygen consumption rate; SRC, spare respiratory capacity; MRC, maximal respiratory capacity.

#1415. Man United 4-4 Aston Villa PLAYER RATINGS: Who looks like the only ray of light at Old Trafford? Whose display was a mess? And which 3/10 star was absolutely hopeless?

Published: 13:52 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 15:31 EST, 8 November 2026

Manchester United will rot 18th in the Premier League table during the international break even after scrambling an unlikely 4-4 draw against Aston Villa.

Michael Carrick's side fought back from a two-goal deficit, inflicted in just four first-half minutes, and went into the interval level after goals from Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans.

They had to pull off the trick a second time after John McGinn's penalty and Leon Goretzka's back-post tap-in made it 4-2 to Unai Emery's visitors.

But Carrick's side refused to throw in the towel despite how hopeless they were for the majority of this game and his substitutes paid off handsomely.

Joshua Zirkzee made it 4-3 in the 92nd minute, teed up by fellow sub Patrick Dorgu, and Dorgu completed the comeback with a 96th-minute finish of his own to send Old Trafford into raptures.

CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox celebrated in the directors' box, all while Emery stormed off down the tunnel before the final whistle.

Daily Mail Sport's NATHAN SALT was in position at Old Trafford to grade both sets of players...

Patrick Dorgu (right) salvaged the most unlikely of points for Manchester United on Sunday

John McGinn (right) was immense but Villa suffered when he went off as they finished 4-4

A mess of a performance. The Belgian got totally muddled up when he tried to save Alysson's first-minute shot with his knees and it flew between his legs. He could then only parry Alysson's shot straight to Jackson, who made it 2-0. Sold short by his defenders for goals three and four but the United malaise seems to have worn down Lammens, who looked so good last season.

Looked like a rabbit in headlights at the start of the game as the ball ricocheted off him en route to Alysson making it 1-0. Did get an assist for cutting the ball back to Tielemans just before half-time but as an overall performance, Villa feasted on his shortcomings.

Looked like the only United defender capable of defending to a respectable level until even he got sucked into the mistake-fest that United put on at the back. A positive first half, in which he made a strong recovery run to deny Jackson racing through for a third goal, was undone when he inexplicably headed onto his own bar under no pressure to gift Villa a fourth as Leon Goretzka turned in the knockdown.

Made a key last-man challenge but otherwise this was another game where he hasn't been able to organise a defence that is crying out for leadership. Forced off at half-time just days after appearing to tweak his hamstring against Roma.

Absolutely hopeless, just as he was against Roma on Tuesday. Switched off in the first minute and made a weak attempt to block Alysson, who scored. Then, two minutes into the second half, he recklessly fouled Alysson to give away a penalty. Many fans cheered when he was substituted. There has to be a better left back solution than Dalot right now.

Thousands of United fans cheered at the announcement that Diogo Dalot was going off

Scored his first goal for United, and against his former side no less. When United were rolling, Tielemans was at the heart of it all. Faded in the second half when Villa took the lead again and he was unsurprisingly taken off as Carrick's first substitution.

Neat and tidy on the ball but got bested by McGinn for the time the Scottish was on the pitch. One of the few who genuinely does look to play forwards when possible.

His goal drought goes on as we rapidly approach a year since his last one. He's electric when he's bearing down on a full-back and he had to score when played in by Tielemans after escaping the sight of Maatsen. Does so much well but his end product simply must improve or he won't merit starts.

Scored a penalty for the second time in a week but cut a frustrated figure for large spells here as the team collapsed. His corner onto the head of Dorgu was the type of quality you need in crunch moments and that's why he rarely comes off.

Looks like the only ray of light these days as this feckless United side fall to even greater depths. Did well to wrestle himself free of Harwood-Bellis to break and win a penalty after a clueless foul from Boubacar Kamara. Stung the palms of Suzuki soon after.

Matheus Cunha dragged United back into the game and did brilliantly to win an early penalty

Didn't do enough to trouble Villa's backline as he once again found himself deployed down the middle. Only took three shots in this basketball-type game.

Could only scratch his chin in disbelief 60 seconds in when Villa took the lead and he looked down and out when it became 4-2 early in the second half. But he was proactive with his substitutions and they all paid off. He deserves credit for that.

Booked for a reckless - and late - lunge. Interesting he got the nod ahead of Matthijs de Ligt at half-time.

Goal and assist off the bench. Has to be the starter at left back from here on out or United will remain in a washing machine cycle of misery defensively.

Drew a furious response when he ballooned a shot over the bar when United were chasing the game late on.

Electric, again. He's fearless and United have needed that this week when the chips were down.

Joshua Zirkzee (for Bryan Mbeumo, 83) - 7

Clinical when the chance came and it was his goal at 4-3 that gave United the opportunity to stage a dramatic late finish. He gives them a focal point that they are crying out for.

Conceded four times and was livid at the end that VAR didn't punish Lammens backing in to him with the last action of the game. It was a performance that saw Suzuki make some huge saves in the first half. There was one big right hand to deny Amad just before half-time and he was also full stretch to tip Cunha's curling shot away, too, just before. Couldn't see Tielemans' equaliser at 2-2 with Mbeumo in front and will feel aggrieved at the finale.

First Premier League start for Villa since his £30million summer switch and he will have not expected for it to come at right back. Found himself in an unfortunate mismatch against Cunha and the ease at which the Brazilian brushed him off shows why it's unlikely to be a long-term assignment given the quality of wide players in the league.

Was so often given the mocking treatment that has now fallen onto the likes of Dalot and Mazraoui during his time at Manchester United but Lindelof is a better player than many here care to admit. Reads the game well and did well to cut out a run into the box by Patrick Dorgu ten minutes from time but was found wanting on the final set piece that triggered the equaliser.

Victor Lindelof is a better player than a lot of United fans may care to admit

Felt like a quarterback for this Villa side for most of it with how many touches he was able to take under very little pressure. Had a big smile on his face for long spells but that was firmly washed off by the end. Abysmal marking as the game entered stoppage time and both Zirkzee and Dorgu scored.

Was given a torrid time by Amad in the first half and still gives opponents too many opportunities to get at him. Shea Lacey had his way with him when he came on, too. Defensively not good enough.

Spent years getting linked to Manchester United but now here as an opposition player, he made them pay with a goal at the Stretford End to make it 4-2. Tidy player.

Idiotic foul to bring Cunha down to give United a lifeline in a game they weren't in 15 minutes in. Seemed to be caught in two minds whether to push onto Tielemans or Mainoo in the 30-minute spell where United looked like a competent football team. Breathed a sigh of relief when the hosts resorted to type.

A total menace that knew within seconds that he had the beating of Dalot each and every time. Clinical strike in the opening minute to give Villa the lead and his trickery and directness paid off a second time at the start of the second half when he baited Dalot into conceding a penalty. Brilliant outing.

Alysson won a penalty after outwitting Diogo Dalot in the United box early in the second half

Best player on the pitch. He made the right decision time after time and even when pressed on the ball when United started to find a groove, he looked to have unshakeable composure. Cool as you like to score a penalty in front of the Stretford End – not least having missed a penalty against Fulham – and then it was his free-kick that led to the fourth. Still feels underrated.

A fearless dribbler that has the potential to be the jewel of this Villa crown in the years to come. In a league that has long ground a lot of flair players down, his physical dribbling through the lines is a sight to behold. Completed more dribbles than any other player by the time he came off.

Quick as a flash to score from Lammens' spill four minutes in and really should have done better when he was played through one v one, only to see Yoro beat him for pace. Led the line in a way that Manchester United were crying out for.

Has never won at Old Trafford as Villa boss and this is the most regrettable of the lot having led both 2-0 and 4-2 here, only to throw it away in both halves. He stormed off furiously before the final whistle.

#1414. Accelerating commercialization and deployment of indoor photovoltaics

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 49–57 (2026) Cite this article

The growing reliance on distributed electronics, such as Internet of Things (IoT) nodes, smart-home devices and portable consumer products, has intensified demand for indoor energy-harvesting technologies that reduce battery replacement and servicing. Consequently, indoor photovoltaics (PVs) have advanced rapidly; however, translating state-of-the-art cells into deployable products requires design principles that reflect real indoor conditions. Here recent progress in perovskite (bulk and quantum dot), organic, amorphous-silicon, III–V and dye-sensitized PVs is examined to identify bottlenecks that arise under low-light conditions and during scale-up. This Review highlights how low-light operation favours wide-bandgap absorbers and reduced non-radiative voltage losses while reshaping module design: lower series-resistance (RS) penalties permit wider subcells and fewer interconnections, increasing geometric fill factor, whereas shunt and leakage pathways consume more of the weak photocurrent. Measurement practices for credible cross-technology benchmarking are discussed, emphasizing the transparent reporting of spectra, illuminance/irradiance, stabilization and uncertainty. Finally, the relationship between device performance and manufacturability and product integration is considered, including power-management requirements and chemical/regulatory constraints (for example, restricted substances and end-of-life handling). These guidelines provide a practical framework for evaluating indoor PVs on the basis of delivered and retained power and for accelerating the transition from laboratory-scale demonstrations to reliable, visually adaptable products for the built environment.
